case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court that had original jurisdiction when it filed and then stayed a case pending arbitration under the FAA retains jurisdiction to decide post-arbitration motions in that same case without identifying a new, independent jurisdictional basis.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. §§ 1–16 (particularly the FAA’s mechanisms for stays and post-award confirmation/vacatur proceedings, including § 10), together with federal subject-matter jurisdiction principles (e.g., original federal-question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 and related supplemental-jurisdiction concepts referenced in briefing, 28 U.S.C. § 1367).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that once a federal court properly has original jurisdiction over a civil action and stays that action pending arbitration, the court’s jurisdiction over the case does not disappear during the stay; therefore, the court may adjudicate post-arbitration motions (e.g., to confirm or vacate the award) within the same stayed case without forcing the parties to establish a fresh, redundant basis for original jurisdiction. Petitioner further contends that multiple circuits have already resolved this question (petitioner says eight), creating sufficient uniformity concerns and that the Second Circuit’s contrary approach is wrong as a matter of jurisdictional continuity and FAA procedure. Petitioner also rejects respondents’ claimed 'vehicle problems,' emphasizing that alternative arguments on jurisdiction and merits are permissible under Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(d).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue the Second Circuit’s decision does not present a mature, well-developed split warranting immediate Supreme Court intervention and, in any event, this case is an imperfect vehicle due to 'factually unique circumstances' and asserted procedural complications. On the merits, respondents’ framing implies that post-arbitration relief (confirmation/vacatur) should be treated as requiring its own jurisdictional footing rather than being automatically available simply because the court once had jurisdiction before imposing the arbitration stay—i.e., a court should not act unless jurisdiction is properly established for the specific post-award request, and the Second Circuit’s handling is defensible under existing jurisdiction doctrines and FAA practice.
key_precedents: Beijing Shougang Mining Inv. Co. v. Mongolia, 11 F.4th 144 (2d Cir. 2021)
Smarter Tools Inc. v. Chongqing SENCI Imp. & Exp. Trade Co., 57 F.4th 372 (2d Cir. 2023)
Weiss v. Sallie Mae, Inc., 939 F.3d 105 (2d Cir. 2019)
Triestman v. Fed. Bureau of Prisons, 470 F.3d 471 (2d Cir. 2006)
MasterCard (case cited by the Second Circuit for comparison, 471 F.3d at 382–83)
Union No. 2 United Ass’n of Journeymen, 841 F.2d 461 (2d Cir. 1988)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: Badgerow requires an independent jurisdictional basis on the face of a §§ 9–11 “application,” and § 3 cannot enlarge Article III power. But that objection assumes the post-award filing is a new, freestanding proceeding; as Justice Barrett emphasizes, § 3’s command to “stay the action” in “the court in which such suit is pending” presupposes a single continuing civil action, and nothing in Badgerow held that jurisdiction properly attached at filing evaporates midstream merely because the merits are sent to arbitration. To avoid any bootstrapping end-run, our holding should be narrow: jurisdiction persists only when the §§ 9–11 request is made by motion in the same stayed case that independently satisfied § 1331/§ 1332 at the outset, leaving Badgerow’s no-look-through rule fully intact for standalone post-award applications. On a minimalist, institutional-legitimacy approach, that line respects statutory text and precedent without creating an atextual “jurisdictional reset” rule that would force duplicative filings and forum churn.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett’s “jurisdictional continuity” theory rests on § 3’s reference to “the court in which such suit is pending,” but that text speaks to where a stay must be entered, not to expanding (or preserving without re-showing) statutory jurisdiction over distinct post-award relief. Badgerow held that §§ 9–11 require an independent jurisdictional basis on the face of the “application,” and recharacterizing those applications as mere in-case motions—because the clerk kept the same docket number—functionally recreates the look-through bootstrapping Badgerow rejected. Ordinary practice about a court’s ability to manage a pending case cannot supply subject-matter jurisdiction Congress did not confer for a particular form of proceeding, and nothing in §§ 9–11 or § 3 says otherwise. Justice Jackson’s point underscores the proper limit: docket mechanics and case-management tools cannot enlarge Article III or the jurisdictional statutes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett’s “jurisdictional continuity” theory draws intuitive force from §3’s reference to “the court in which such suit is pending,” but that language speaks to which court must issue a stay; it does not purport to eliminate the independent jurisdictional showing Badgerow requires for §§9–11 “applications.” Treating post-award confirmation/vacatur as merely a case-management step because it is filed under the same docket number effectively allows the stayed merits complaint to function as a perpetual jurisdictional anchor—precisely the kind of functional look-through bootstrapping Justice Jackson warns against, and which Badgerow rejected absent clear congressional authorization. Ordinary practice that a court retains jurisdiction to “complete” a case cannot override the statutory structure that makes §§9–11 a distinct form of relief triggered by an “application” and not jurisdiction-conferring on its own. Whatever the practical inconvenience, we should not expand federal adjudicatory power based on docket continuity rather than an on-the-face jurisdictional basis for the post-award application.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Thomas press the best point: Badgerow’s insistence that §§ 9–11 "applications" show an independent jurisdictional basis, and that § 3 cannot be used to bootstrap federal power. But that critique assumes the post-award filing initiates a new proceeding; as Justice Barrett emphasizes, § 3’s command that “the court in which such suit is pending” must “stay the action” presupposes the same Article III case remains pending, and nothing in Badgerow holds that jurisdiction properly attached at filing evaporates midstream because the court compelled arbitration. The anti-bootstrapping worry is substantially answered by cabining the rule to post-award motions filed in the same stayed docket (not freestanding applications), which preserves Badgerow’s no-look-through limit while avoiding a formalistic, resource-draining forum reset that disproportionately burdens less-resourced parties. Under my pragmatic approach, absent a clear statutory direction to force that reset, I would treat post-award confirmation/vacatur here as part of completing an already-jurisdictional case rather than as a new jurisdiction-conferring suit.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s bootstrapping point is the hardest: parties might file a jurisdiction-invoking merits suit, obtain a § 3 stay, and then secure a federal forum for §§ 9–10 relief that Badgerow would deny if filed standalone. But as Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice emphasize, § 3’s directive to “stay the action” in “the court in which such suit is pending” most naturally treats the post-award motion in that same docket as a continuation of an already-proper Article III case, not a new “application” commencing a new jurisdictional proceeding. Justice Thomas’s “distinct remedies” framing identifies that §§ 9–11 are separate forms of relief, yet it does not show Congress clearly required a midstream jurisdictional reset or divestiture once jurisdiction properly attached—Badgerow’s rule remains fully operative for freestanding post-award applications, while continuity here is a narrow, administrable line consistent with ordinary federal practice. On my pragmatic textualist approach, we should not infer an atextual jurisdiction-stripping consequence from the FAA that would force duplicative refiling and forum shuffling without clear statutory command.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: Badgerow demands jurisdiction on the face of a §§ 9–11 “application,” and a § 3 stay cannot manufacture federal power for post-award relief. But Justice Barrett’s textual focus on § 3—directing “the court in which such suit is pending” to “stay the action”—best reflects ordinary procedural meaning: the same Article III “case” remains pending, and nothing in §§ 9–11 clearly commands a midstream jurisdictional reset or divestiture once jurisdiction properly attached at filing. Treating an in-docket post-award motion as a new, freestanding proceeding would add a jurisdiction-stripping rule Congress did not write, while our narrow holding (as the Chief Justice suggests) leaves Badgerow fully intact for standalone confirmation/vacatur actions newly commenced after arbitration. The anti-bootstrapping concern is real, but on a textualist/originalist approach it cannot justify recharacterizing “pending suit” continuity as jurisdictional evaporation absent a clear statutory directive.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Jackson press the best objection: Badgerow says a §§ 9–11 “application” must show an independent jurisdictional basis on its face, and § 3 cannot expand Article III power. But that framing, as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, wrongly treats an in-docket post-award motion as a new, freestanding proceeding rather than a continuation of a properly invoked federal “suit” that § 3 keeps “pending” via a stay. On ordinary federal practice and an institutional view, jurisdiction that properly attached at filing does not evaporate midstream absent a clear divestiture; Badgerow’s rule sensibly governs standalone post-award filings, not a stayed case returning for final disposition. The anti-bootstrapping concern is real, but it is answered by a narrow holding limited to post-award motions filed in the same stayed action, which preserves Badgerow’s line and avoids an atextual, inefficient jurisdictional reset.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Jackson present the strongest textual objection: Badgerow insists that §§ 9–11 “applications” need an independent jurisdictional basis, and § 3 does not itself confer jurisdiction. But that argument assumes the post-award filing is a new, freestanding proceeding; § 3’s command to “stay the action” in “the court in which such suit is pending” presupposes the same civil action remains pending within the court’s already-attached § 1331/§ 1332 jurisdiction, absent a clear divestiture. Reading “application” in §§ 9–11 to require a midstream jurisdictional reset when the parties return to the same stayed docket would add an atextual jurisdiction-stripping consequence to § 3’s mandatory stay, rather than faithfully applying Badgerow’s no-look-through rule for standalone, newly commenced post-award actions. Chief Justice Roberts’s continuity framing thus answers the bootstrapping concern by limiting the holding to motions filed in the same case—preserving Badgerow’s boundary while respecting ordinary jurisdictional retention once properly invoked.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s “jurisdictional continuity” theory has real pragmatic appeal, especially where § 3 describes “the court in which such suit is pending,” and I appreciate Justice Sotomayor’s fairness concern about forcing costly refiling. But their approach still treats docket mechanics as doing jurisdictional work that Badgerow says §§ 9–11 “applications” must do on their own face; limiting the rule to “same docket” does not eliminate the bootstrapping problem Justice Thomas identifies—it just narrows the pathway. In my view, §§ 9–11 create distinct forms of post-award relief that Congress did not make jurisdiction-conferring, and § 3’s stay cannot convert that absence into federal power without effectively reintroducing a look-through-like end run. A bright-line requirement for an independent jurisdictional basis at the post-award stage better enforces statutory limits and procedural fairness by preventing strategic forum anchoring through an initial merits filing.

John Roberts.reasoning: A district court that properly exercised original jurisdiction over a filed civil action does not lose that jurisdiction merely because it entered a mandatory stay under FAA § 3; the case remains on the court’s docket, and the court may resolve post-arbitration motions as part of the same Article III “case or controversy” without requiring a new, independent jurisdictional hook. Badgerow’s bar on “look-through” jurisdiction for standalone FAA §§ 9–10 applications is best read to govern new, freestanding confirmation/vacatur proceedings, not post-award motions made in an already-pending federal action that was stayed pending arbitration. That narrower reading respects Badgerow and Vaden while avoiding needless procedural duplication and promoting institutional legitimacy through a limited ruling tied to § 3’s stay mechanism. The FAA contains no instruction that a § 3 stay terminates the court’s adjudicatory power over the existing action, and treating the post-award phase as a continuation of the same suit better fits ordinary federal practice concerning stayed cases and ancillary proceedings.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FAA is "something of an anomaly" that does not itself confer subject-matter jurisdiction, so a federal court may act under §§ 9–11 only when an independent jurisdictional basis appears on the face of the application. Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), rejected using the underlying merits dispute to supply jurisdiction for §§ 9–10 proceedings, and nothing in § 3’s stay mechanism textually extends federal jurisdiction to post-award confirmation/vacatur absent that independent basis. A stayed case pauses merits adjudication; it does not enlarge Article III jurisdiction, and ancillary jurisdiction cannot be used to circumvent the jurisdictional limits Badgerow enforced. Because the post-award motions seek new relief under §§ 9–10, the district court must identify a valid jurisdictional hook (e.g., § 1331 or diversity) for those motions themselves.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Badgerow v. Walters, 142 S. Ct. 1310 (2022), holds that applications under FAA §§ 9–11 (including § 10 vacatur) require an independent basis for federal jurisdiction apparent on the face of the application, and courts may not rely on the nature of the underlying dispute to supply jurisdiction. Nothing in FAA § 3’s stay mechanism purports to confer continuing Article III jurisdiction to decide later, distinct post-award relief; a stay pauses proceedings but does not expand federal courts’ limited jurisdiction, and practical consequences counsel against allowing parties to bootstrap federal jurisdiction indefinitely from an earlier filing. Treating confirmation/vacatur as requiring its own jurisdictional footing also aligns with the FAA’s structure, which creates specific post-award “application” procedures rather than automatic continuation of the original merits case. Accordingly, absent a fresh jurisdictional basis for the §§ 9–11 request, the district court should not act simply because it once had jurisdiction before ordering arbitration.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: When a district court properly exercises original jurisdiction over a filed civil action (e.g., under 28 U.S.C. § 1331) and issues a stay pending arbitration under FAA § 3, that stay pauses merits litigation but does not dissolve the court’s subject-matter jurisdiction over the already-pending case; the court may therefore resolve post-award motions within that same docket as part of administering its judgment and providing effective relief. Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), is best read as addressing jurisdiction for freestanding FAA §§ 9–11 applications filed as new actions (rejecting “look-through” jurisdiction there), not as stripping jurisdiction from a court that already has it and simply stayed proceedings. Forcing parties—often employees or consumers with limited resources—into duplicative filings or state-court relitigation after a federal stay would undermine access to justice and frustrate the FAA’s stay mechanism’s practical function. Nothing in the FAA’s text (including § 10) requires a new, independent jurisdictional showing for post-award motions brought in the same stayed case where jurisdiction was secure at the outset.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: A stay under FAA § 3 pauses proceedings but does not terminate the civil action, so a district court that properly exercised original jurisdiction at filing (e.g., under 28 U.S.C. § 1331) retains that jurisdiction to resolve later motions in the same case, including FAA § 10 vacatur or § 9 confirmation. Badgerow v. Walters held only that a freestanding, post-award § 9/§ 10 application cannot invoke “look-through” jurisdiction; it did not address (and had no occasion to address) post-award relief sought within an already-pending federal action stayed for arbitration. Treating post-award motions in the stayed case as requiring a brand-new jurisdictional basis would create an impractical, formalistic discontinuity that the FAA’s stay mechanism (§ 3) is designed to avoid and would undermine coherent case management. Vaden’s look-through framework is likewise inapposite here because jurisdiction derives from the existing federal case, not from an independent FAA “petition” initiating federal court involvement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: A stay under FAA §3 keeps the “action” pending; it does not terminate the case or divest the court of the subject-matter jurisdiction that properly attached at filing under 28 U.S.C. §1331 (or other original-jurisdiction grants). Nothing in FAA §§9–11, including §10, demands a new, freestanding jurisdictional hook to resolve post-award motions when they are made in the same already-jurisdictional civil action; ordinary jurisdictional continuity and the separation-of-powers baseline (courts exercise jurisdiction Congress has conferred, and that jurisdiction persists until final disposition) point the other way. Badgerow v. Walters held only that the FAA does not itself create jurisdiction for standalone, post-arbitration applications filed as new actions, not that jurisdiction evaporates midstream in an existing federal case stayed under §3. Reading the FAA to require parties to relitigate jurisdiction (or to split proceedings across federal and state courts) after a §3 stay lacks textual grounding and invites the incoherent, two-track regime the statute’s stay-and-enforcement scheme was designed to avoid.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A §3 stay under the FAA pauses—rather than terminates—the civil action, so a district court that properly exercised original jurisdiction at filing retains jurisdiction to take later steps in the same case, including ruling on post-arbitration motions under §§ 9–10 without requiring a new, redundant jurisdictional hook. That understanding best fits ordinary federal practice concerning stayed cases and avoids impractical, wasteful “start over” litigation that would undermine the FAA’s pro-arbitration, streamlined design. Badgerow v. Walters addressed a different posture—an independent, newly filed confirmation/vacatur proceeding—and does not compel treating post-award motions within an already-filed, stayed federal action as jurisdictionally new. Consistent with Moses H. Cone Memorial Hospital v. Mercury Construction Corp.’s emphasis on the FAA’s efficient “piecemeal” arbitration process and practical workability, continuing jurisdiction here promotes finality and judicial restraint by keeping enforcement in the same case rather than spawning ancillary litigation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3’s text directs that “the court in which such suit is pending” must stay the “action until such arbitration has been had,” which presupposes the action remains pending in the same court during the stay rather than terminating for jurisdictional purposes. Consistent with Green Tree Financial Corp.-Alabama v. Randolph and Smith v. Spizzirri, a stay keeps the case on the district court’s docket so the parties may return to that court if arbitration fails or for subsequent proceedings; requiring a new, independent jurisdictional basis to decide post-award motions within the same stayed action is in tension with that structure. Badgerow correctly holds that the FAA does not itself create federal jurisdiction for a freestanding confirmation/vacatur application, but that rule does not compel treating post-arbitration motions filed in the already-pending, jurisdictionally proper civil action as a new case requiring a redundant jurisdictional showing. Where original subject-matter jurisdiction existed at filing (e.g., § 1331) and the action remains pending under § 3, the district court retains jurisdiction to adjudicate the post-arbitration motions in that case, subject to ordinary limits on its jurisdiction and any applicable precedent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), makes clear that FAA §§ 9–10 applications require an independent jurisdictional basis appearing on the face of the post-award application, and the court may not rely on the federal character of the underlying dispute to supply jurisdiction. A § 3 stay pauses merits litigation but does not itself expand Article III and statutory subject-matter jurisdiction; treating the stayed complaint as a perpetual jurisdictional “anchor” would effectively create an end-run around Badgerow’s jurisdictional limits and blur the line between continuing case management and new, post-award relief. Ancillary or supplemental jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. § 1367) does not comfortably fit where the confirmation/vacatur request is a distinct statutory proceeding under the FAA with its own jurisdictional rule, and practical consequences favor clear, administrable jurisdictional boundaries that preserve procedural fairness. Accordingly, absent a new independent basis (e.g., diversity) on the face of the § 9/§ 10 request, the district court lacks jurisdiction to decide post-arbitration motions in the stayed action.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court that properly had original jurisdiction over a case may, after staying that same pending case for arbitration under the Federal Arbitration Act, decide post-arbitration motions (e.g., confirmation/vacatur) without identifying a new, independent basis for federal subject-matter jurisdiction.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. §§ 1–16 (especially §§ 9–10 on confirmation/vacatur and § 3 on stays), and federal subject-matter jurisdiction principles (including supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367 as referenced in the briefing).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that once a federal court properly has original jurisdiction and issues a stay pending arbitration, it retains jurisdiction in that same ongoing case to adjudicate post-arbitration motions without needing to plead a separate, redundant jurisdictional basis. Petitioner contends the Second Circuit’s contrary approach is wrong as a matter of FAA structure and ordinary civil procedure (a stayed case remains on the court’s docket), creates inefficiency and potential forum manipulation by forcing parties into a separate jurisdictional showing or new proceeding, and conflicts with how multiple circuits treat jurisdiction in stayed, continuing actions. Petitioner also disputes alleged 'vehicle problems,' noting that alternative arguments are permitted (Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(d)) and that the issue is cleanly presented.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue the Second Circuit’s decision does not warrant Supreme Court intervention now, characterizing any circuit split as weak/underdeveloped and asserting this case is a poor vehicle due to allegedly unique factual/procedural circumstances and purported 'vehicle problems.' On the merits, respondents’ framing implies that post-arbitration relief under the FAA (confirmation/vacatur) requires its own jurisdictional footing even if the federal court earlier had original jurisdiction and stayed the action, and that courts must be attentive to the FAA’s jurisdictional limits rather than assuming continuing federal power after arbitration. Respondents also contend petitioner’s predicted harms (forum shopping/inefficiency) are speculative.
key_precedents: Beijing Shougang Mining Inv. Co. v. Mongolia, 11 F.4th 144 (2d Cir. 2021)
Smarter Tools Inc. v. Chongqing SENCI Imp. & Exp. Trade Co., 57 F.4th 372 (2d Cir. 2023)
Weiss v. Sallie Mae, Inc., 939 F.3d 105 (2d Cir. 2019)
Triestman v. Fed. Bureau of Prisons, 470 F.3d 471 (2d Cir. 2006)
Union No. 2 United Ass’n of Journeymen, 841 F.2d 461 (2d Cir. 1988)
MasterCard (as cited in the Second Circuit excerpt: 471 F.3d at 382–83)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is that Badgerow demands an independent jurisdictional basis for any §§ 9–10 request, to prevent federal jurisdiction from being expanded by characterization. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, FAA § 3 stays “the action,” and Smith v. Spizzirri confirms the stay keeps the same case pending so parties may return for further judicial steps—making post-award confirmation/vacatur in that same docket ancillary to an already-valid Article III case rather than a new freestanding “application.” Justice Kavanaugh’s observation about § 1367 reinforces (without needing to decide it) that these post-award motions arise from the same case or controversy once original jurisdiction attached, and nothing in the FAA or Title 28 clearly strips that jurisdiction midstream. A narrow holding limited to post-award motions filed in the same stayed action preserves Badgerow for standalone applications and avoids unnecessary disruption and gamesmanship, consistent with institutional legitimacy and minimalism.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention—rooted in Badgerow—that every §§ 9–10 request must independently satisfy jurisdiction treats a post-award motion in a stayed case as if it were a new civil action, but the FAA’s text does not do that. As Justice Alito notes, § 3 commands the court to “stay the trial of the action,” and a stay presupposes a continuing Article III case rather than a terminated proceeding that must be re-invoked. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Smith v. Spizzirri reinforces that Congress chose a stay (not dismissal) so parties may “return” to the same court; nothing in the FAA or Title 28 strips jurisdiction midstream absent a clear jurisdiction-stripping directive. Badgerow remains limited to freestanding post-award “applications” and cannot be extended atextually to impose a jurisdictional reset where original jurisdiction already properly attached.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—reading Badgerow to require an independent jurisdictional basis for every §§ 9–10 request—fails once we keep the statutory posture in view: FAA § 3 directs the court to “stay the trial of the action,” which presupposes the same federal case remains pending rather than dissolving into a new freestanding proceeding. Chief Justice Roberts’s framing is the most persuasive: a post-award confirmation/vacatur motion filed on the stayed docket is ancillary to an already-valid Article III case, and jurisdiction does not evaporate absent a jurisdiction-stripping event. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Smith v. Spizzirri strengthens the textual and practical inference that Congress chose a stay precisely so the parties can return to the same court for necessary post-arbitration steps, making respondent’s jurisdictional “reset” both atextual and disruptive. Extending Badgerow beyond standalone applications would invite inefficiency and manipulation without any clear command in the FAA or Title 28.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent point remains that Badgerow treats §§ 9–10 as a distinct “application” requiring its own jurisdictional basis, but that collapses the critical § 3 procedural posture: a mandatory stay keeps the same civil action pending, and there is no jurisdiction-stripping event that would make Article III jurisdiction “evaporate” midstream. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Smith v. Spizzirri is particularly persuasive to me because it underscores Congress’s choice of a stay (not dismissal) precisely so parties can return to the same court for the necessary follow-on steps—an understanding that avoids extending Badgerow beyond standalone petitions. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan also correctly emphasize that this narrow holding preserves Badgerow while preventing wasteful refiling and strategic jurisdictional maneuvering that would disproportionately burden less-resourced litigants. I do not see any textual command in the FAA or Title 28 that compels respondent’s more formalistic reset.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent point—grounded in Badgerow’s “face of the application” rule—is that §§ 9–10 are always jurisdictionally freestanding, even when filed after arbitration, but that overreads Badgerow beyond the standalone-application posture it decided and ignores § 3’s textual premise that the court stays “the action,” not ends it. Chief Justice Roberts’s framing is most persuasive to me: in the § 3-stay posture, confirmation/vacatur is an ancillary step in the same pending Article III case, so there is no principled “jurisdictional reset” absent a jurisdiction-stripping event. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Smith v. Spizzirri reinforces that structural design—Congress chose a stay so parties can return to federal court—which would be incoherent if jurisdiction evaporated midstream. A narrow rule limited to post-award motions filed in the same stayed action preserves Badgerow for truly standalone petitions while avoiding atextual, inefficient dismissal-and-refile gamesmanship.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressing Badgerow’s “independent jurisdictional basis” requirement across all §§ 9–10 requests—fails in the § 3 posture because the statute commands a stay of “the action,” not its termination; nothing in the FAA effects a jurisdiction-stripping event midstream. Chief Justice Roberts’s framing is decisive: a post-award confirmation/vacatur request filed on the same stayed docket is best understood as a continuation of an already-valid Article III case, not a new freestanding proceeding that must re-establish jurisdiction. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Smith v. Spizzirri reinforces that original understanding of § 3 stays as preserving the case so parties may return for further judicial steps, which is incompatible with respondent’s jurisdictional “reset” theory. Reading Badgerow to compel a second jurisdictional hook here would extend its holding beyond standalone applications and add an atextual formality unsupported by the FAA’s text or ordinary federal practice.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent point—invoking Badgerow’s “face of the application” rule as a categorical requirement for §§ 9–10—fails to account for the § 3 posture: a stay preserves the same pending “action,” so the court is exercising continuing jurisdiction it already properly had, not adjudicating a new freestanding FAA proceeding. Chief Justice Roberts’s framing is persuasive on ordinary federal practice and Article III: jurisdiction does not evaporate midstream absent a jurisdiction-stripping event, and treating the post-award motion as ancillary to the stayed case avoids atextual formalism and gamesmanship. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Smith v. Spizzirri meaningfully strengthens the textual/structural inference that Congress chose a stay so parties can “return to federal court” for further judicial steps, which is hard to reconcile with a requirement to re-establish jurisdiction after arbitration. Badgerow remains fully respected on its own facts (standalone post-award applications); extending it to stayed cases would be an unnecessary and disruptive expansion not compelled by text or precedent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument remains that Badgerow’s “face of the application” rule for §§ 9–10 should apply categorically because those provisions do not themselves confer jurisdiction; but that would extend Badgerow beyond its posture of freestanding, post-award applications and ignore the procedural consequence of an FAA § 3 stay. Chief Justice Roberts’s framing is decisive for me: § 3 directs the court to stay “the action,” which in ordinary legal usage presupposes a continuing case on the docket rather than a terminated proceeding that must be re-initiated with a new jurisdictional basis. Justice Kagan and Justice Alito reinforce that nothing in the FAA or Title 28 purports to divest jurisdiction midstream, and Smith v. Spizzirri supports the structural understanding that the stay is meant to permit the parties to return to the same court for further steps. On a textualist and originalist approach, absent a clear jurisdiction-stripping command, I see no basis to impose an atextual “jurisdictional reset” when the post-award motion is filed in the same stayed action.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest respondent point—that Badgerow demands an independent jurisdictional basis for every §§ 9–10 request—has force as a formal jurisdictional rule, but it overlooks the procedural posture Congress created in FAA § 3: the court stays “the action,” and a stay ordinarily preserves a single continuing case rather than initiating a new one. Chief Justice Roberts’s framing is most persuasive to me because it treats post-award confirmation/vacatur filed on the stayed docket as ancillary steps in an already-proper Article III case, which avoids wasteful refiling and jurisdictional gamesmanship without expanding federal power beyond the jurisdiction validly invoked at the outset. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Smith v. Spizzirri matters because it reinforces the structural expectation that parties may “return” to the same federal court after arbitration—an expectation that becomes incoherent if jurisdiction silently evaporates absent any jurisdiction-stripping command. On my pragmatic, fairness-centered approach, Badgerow should remain controlling for freestanding post-award applications, but it should not be extended to impose an atextual jurisdictional reset midstream in a stayed federal action.

John Roberts.reasoning: Where a district court properly exercised original jurisdiction over the underlying action and stayed that same case under FAA § 3, the post-arbitration request to confirm or vacate is best understood as a continuation of the existing Article III “case,” not a new freestanding FAA proceeding requiring a redundant jurisdictional showing. Badgerow v. Walters limited “look-through” jurisdiction for standalone §§ 9–10 applications, but it did not address (and should not be extended to unsettle) the court’s authority to resolve post-arbitration motions within a stayed federal action that remains on the docket. This narrower path respects the FAA’s structure (§ 3’s stay mechanism) while preserving institutional legitimacy by avoiding a rule that would force dismissal and refiling gamesmanship after federal jurisdiction was properly invoked at the outset. The court can thus decide confirmation/vacatur without identifying a new independent jurisdictional basis, so long as the original federal jurisdiction remains intact and the matter is pursued in the same stayed case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III and the jurisdictional statutes grant federal courts power over "Cases" within their original jurisdiction, and nothing in the FAA’s text suggests that a court loses that power merely by entering a stay under 9 U.S.C. § 3; a stayed action remains the same case on the docket. Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), held only that FAA §§ 9–10 do not themselves supply jurisdiction for a new, freestanding post-arbitration application and rejected “look-through” jurisdiction outside § 4; it does not require a new jurisdictional showing when post-award motions are filed in the same action already properly before the court. Where original jurisdiction existed at filing (e.g., under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 or 1332), adjudicating confirmation/vacatur in that ongoing case is at least permissible as part of the same case, consistent with ordinary jurisdictional principles and (as argued) 28 U.S.C. § 1367’s grant over related proceedings. The Second Circuit’s contrary rule imposes atextual jurisdictional hurdles not found in the FAA or Title 28 and improperly treats post-award motions as a separate lawsuit rather than a continuation of the stayed case.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3 of the FAA expressly contemplates that the district court will "stay the trial of the action" while arbitration proceeds, which presupposes the same civil action remains pending on the court’s docket and within its original subject-matter jurisdiction; nothing in §§ 9–10 requires a new, freestanding jurisdictional grant when the court is acting in the same stayed case. Badgerow v. Walters held only that a standalone §§ 9–10 application must show an independent jurisdictional basis on its face, rejecting Vaden’s look-through for new post-arbitration proceedings, but it did not address (and should not be extended to) the distinct posture where a federal court already properly has original jurisdiction and merely resumes adjudication after a § 3 stay. Requiring parties to re-plead jurisdiction or start a new action after arbitration would be atextual and would create serious practical inefficiencies and opportunities for gamesmanship inconsistent with the FAA’s structure favoring streamlined enforcement. Because the district court’s authority here is best understood as part of continuing jurisdiction over the original case, post-arbitration motions to confirm or vacate can be resolved without identifying a new, independent jurisdictional hook.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: When a district court properly exercises original jurisdiction and enters a stay under FAA § 3, the case remains pending on the court’s docket, and the court’s authority to proceed to the post-arbitration phase (confirmation/vacatur under §§ 9–10) is best understood as part of the same civil action rather than a new, freestanding jurisdictional proceeding. Badgerow v. Walters limits federal jurisdiction over standalone § 9/§ 10 applications and rejects “look-through,” but it does not require courts to manufacture a second, independent jurisdictional hook to resolve motions in a case over which they already had jurisdiction and merely stayed. Requiring a new jurisdictional basis after a § 3 stay would invite inefficiency and strategic behavior, undermining access to justice for parties least able to relitigate procedural hurdles, while offering no clear statutory command in the FAA to strip jurisdiction midstream. Consistent with Cortez Byrd Chips, Inc. v. Bill Harbert Constr. Co., a court that had jurisdiction to stay an action for arbitration retains sufficient continuing jurisdiction to resolve the ensuing award-related motions in that same action.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3 of the FAA directs the district court to "stay the trial of the action" pending arbitration, which ordinarily presupposes a single continuing civil action on the court’s docket rather than a jurisdictional reset after arbitration; in that posture, post-award confirmation/vacatur is best understood as ancillary to the existing case over which the court properly had original jurisdiction. Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), held that a freestanding §§ 9–10 application must itself establish an independent jurisdictional basis on its face, but it did not address (and should not be read to silently displace) the court’s continuing authority to resolve post-arbitration motions in the same stayed action that began with unquestioned federal-question or diversity jurisdiction. Reading the FAA to require a new, duplicative jurisdictional showing after a § 3 stay would undermine workability and invite inefficient procedural maneuvering without clear textual command, and it would sit uneasily with the FAA’s structure treating the court’s role as supervisory in a stayed case. This narrower holding preserves Badgerow’s face-of-the-application rule for standalone petitions while maintaining coherent, administrable federal jurisdiction in stayed actions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: A stay under FAA § 3 keeps the civil action pending on the district court’s docket; it does not terminate the case or divest the court of the subject-matter jurisdiction it properly possessed at the outset. Nothing in FAA §§ 9–10 demands that a party identify a new, independent jurisdictional hook to seek confirmation or vacatur when those motions are filed in the same stayed action, and reading such a requirement into the statute would add atextual hurdles and invite wasteful duplicative filings. Our decision in Smith v. Spizzirri confirms § 3’s function is to preserve the court’s continuing supervisory role so the parties may return if arbitration fails or to facilitate recovery on an award, which coheres with ordinary federal practice in stayed cases. At minimum, once original jurisdiction exists over the underlying dispute, post-arbitration motions in that same action fall within the court’s continuing authority, and any contrary rule would improperly elevate form over the jurisdiction already established.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A Section 3 stay keeps the original federal case on the court’s docket, and nothing in FAA §§ 9–10 affirmatively requires a second, redundant jurisdictional showing for post-arbitration motions filed in that same action. Badgerow v. Walters holds that FAA §§ 9–11 applications need an independent jurisdictional basis when they are brought as standalone proceedings, but it does not compel the conclusion that a court must reestablish jurisdiction midstream in a properly commenced, stayed case. In addition, 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) supports continuing adjudicatory authority over post-arbitration confirmation/vacatur motions that form part of the same Article III “case or controversy” once original jurisdiction properly attached. Practically, forcing a new jurisdictional hook after a stay would undermine workability and invite inefficiency and forum manipulation, contrary to the FAA’s pro-arbitration structure and ordinary federal procedure.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3 of the FAA directs that once a suit is referable to arbitration, the court “shall” stay the action “until … arbitration has been had,” which in ordinary procedural terms keeps the same case on the court’s docket rather than terminating it. Smith v. Spizzirri confirms that a requested § 3 stay is mandatory and explains that the stay mechanism exists so “the parties can return to federal court” if arbitration fails or further judicial action is needed, strongly implying continuing adjudicatory authority in the same action after the award. Requiring a new, independent subject-matter-jurisdiction showing for post-award motions in that stayed case would be in tension with § 3’s text and structure and with the baseline principle that a properly invoked original jurisdiction does not evaporate mid-case absent some jurisdiction-stripping event. Badgerow’s limits on jurisdiction for standalone §§ 9–10 applications do not compel a different result where the federal court is acting within an already-valid, stayed civil action rather than entertaining a new, freestanding proceeding.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: A district court that properly exercised original jurisdiction and then entered a § 3 stay keeps the same case on its docket; as a matter of ordinary civil procedure and procedural fairness, it should be able to resolve the parties’ post-arbitration confirmation/vacatur motions in that continuing action without forcing a duplicative “new” jurisdictional hook. Cortez Byrd Chips recognizes that “the court with the power to stay the action under § 3 … has the further power to confirm any ensuing arbitration award,” which fits the FAA’s structure treating post-award relief under §§ 9–10 as part of implementing the arbitration in the stayed case. Requiring a fresh, independent subject-matter showing after arbitration would elevate formalism over practical consequences, inviting inefficiency and gamesmanship while providing no clear statutory command in the FAA to divest jurisdiction midstream. This approach is also consistent with the FAA’s limited jurisdictional design (as emphasized in cases like Badgerow) because it relies on the court’s already-established original jurisdiction over the underlying action, not a “look-through” or newly manufactured basis.
